site.name: WNH
site.tagline: Design systems, built to outlast the designer.
site.manifesto: We don't just deliver designs; we build the infrastructure for them. Our systems let non-designers hold the brand together long after we've gone.
site.studioCopy: WNH works across identity, campaign, exhibition, 3D and film — and builds the guidelines, templates and tools that keep all of it consistent once it's in your team's hands.
site.availability: Taking on two projects for Q1 2027.

portfolio.lead: Identity systems, campaign and event design, exhibitions, 3D and live broadcast — and the guidelines and tools that keep them consistent afterwards. Available for design direction, and for the kind of role where making and leading are the same job.
portfolio.note: Full case studies, references and the long version on request.
portfolio.statement: I've shot in an operating theatre, run a live broadcast gallery, modelled a chainsaw and drawn a logistics icon set. What links them isn't the craft — it's that in every case somebody had to keep it going after I left. Building the thing that lets them is the part of the job I actually love.

projects.title: Asia Breakthrough Growth
projects.role: Live Stream Technical Lead, Motion Graphics
projects.summary: Milwaukee's largest Asia event of 2022, staged as a live broadcast — the multi-camera gallery, the motion graphics package, and the whole technical chain from camera to stream.

cover.alt: Milwaukee Asia Breakthrough Growth live broadcast

blocks.heading: The brief
blocks.body:
Asia Breakthrough Growth was Milwaukee's largest regional event of 2022, and it was built to be watched live rather than reported afterwards. That decision changes everything upstream: there is no edit to fix a mistake in, and no second pass at a graphic that missed its cue.

Two roles on the same show — technical lead on the live stream, and designer of the motion graphics package running through it.

blocks.alt: Broadcast gallery during Asia Breakthrough Growth
blocks.caption: Multi-camera gallery, live to region

blocks.heading: One take, no post
blocks.body:
A broadcast graphics package is not a video. It has to be built as a set of states that can be called on cue, hold at any length, and survive being cut to from a camera that arrived a beat early.

The technical chain — cameras, switching, encoding, stream — had to hold for the full run of the show, in a room full of people who could not be asked to wait.

blocks.caption: Product reveal, presenter position, floor team

blocks.heading: Owning both ends
blocks.body:
Designing the graphics and running the stream is usually two people in two rooms. Doing both meant the package was designed around what the switcher could actually do, and the show was cut around what the graphics needed.

On a live show that is the difference between a graphic that lands and a graphic that arrives late.

projects.title: A Century of Clinical Excellence
projects.role: Commemorative Design, 3D, Exhibition Structure, Live Broadcast Lead
projects.summary: The centenary of Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital, held in a year when nobody could gather — a live-streamed ceremony I led end to end, a 3D centenary mark built as a real object and filled by hand, and a heritage-museum exhibition that had to stand without touching the building.

credits.name: Hong Kong Museum of Medical Sciences

blocks.heading: A hundred years, in the year nobody could gather
blocks.body:
Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital turned a hundred in 2022 — 醫護傳承 · 卓越百年, A Century of Clinical Excellence.

A centenary of that size is normally a hall full of people. Covid took the hall away. So the whole thing had to happen down a wire: no audience, no crowd shot, no room to carry the moment. What replaced it was a live stream, and I led that project end to end — the plan, the setup, the run of show and the technical build, not just the graphics that went into it.

That is an unusual pairing and a useful one. Ceremony graphics are normally designed for a room and then fall apart on a stream. Here the same person who designed what was on the stage was responsible for how it reached everyone who could not be there, so everything was built already knowing what a camera and a compressed feed would do to it.

blocks.heading: A mark you could pour into
blocks.body:
The centenary mark was modelled in 3D before it was drawn flat, because it had to exist as a physical object on the stage — a hollow, transparent 100 with the hospital's crest set inside the second zero.

Hollow, because the ceremony needed something to do. Instead of a ribbon or a switch, the officiating guests poured small green beads into the numeral until it filled and lit up. 凝聚力 — many separate grains, no single one of them the story, becoming one solid form. A hundred years of a hospital is exactly that: thousands of people's shifts, poured in one at a time.

It also solved the streaming problem. A pour is slow, physical and legible on a small screen, and it gives a camera something to move on when there is no applause to cut to. Designing the mark as an object first meant the printed version inherited the real thing's proportions, rather than the sculpture being a thickened copy of a logo.

items.alt: The 3D centenary mark in model view, filled with green granules
The centenary mark modelled in 3D, side view
The finished sculpture in place for the ceremony

blocks.caption: Modelled, then made — and filled by hand on the day

blocks.heading: An exhibition that could not touch the building
blocks.body:
The historical showcase went into the Hong Kong Museum of Medical Sciences — which is itself a declared monument, an Edwardian institute building with its own arched windows, floors and plaster to answer for.

So the brief had a hard constraint before it had a subject: nothing may be fixed to the fabric. No wall anchors, no drilling, no load on anything historic. I worked out the structure around that — a free-standing system of panels that carries its own weight, holds the graphics and the vitrines, threads through the existing rooms and comes out again leaving the monument exactly as it was found.

That is why the whole thing was resolved in 3D first. Exhibition work is unforgiving in a way print is not: a wrong measurement is not a reprint, it is a carpenter — and in a protected building it is also a conversation you do not want to have.

items.alt: The free-standing exhibition structure resolved in 3D
Graphic panels and archive vitrines as built
Historic nurse's uniform on display inside the museum

blocks.caption: The 3D plan, and the same structure standing in the museum

blocks.heading: One year, told three ways
blocks.body:
The exhibition set out a hundred years of the hospital's part in medicine in Hong Kong — care, medical education and clinical research — through the objects that survived it: instruments, uniforms, photographs, paperwork.

Between the stream, the sculpture and the showcase, the centenary reached three different audiences in three different ways and still read as one year rather than six separate jobs.

items.alt: The broadcast set, cameras and crew around the centenary mark

blocks.caption: Online showcase, and the broadcast set on the day

projects.title: Sixty Years of Management
projects.summary: A 60th-anniversary identity for the Hong Kong Management Association, extended into an interview platform carrying over a hundred leadership insights from Hong Kong business leaders.

blocks.heading: An anniversary that had to do work
blocks.body: The Hong Kong Management Association turned sixty. The mark was built on a construction grid with clear-space and colour rules from the start, because it was going to spend a year being applied by people who are not designers — event teams, printers, partner organisations.

blocks.alt: HKMA 60 mark with construction grid and clear space
blocks.caption: Construction, clear space, colour

blocks.heading: From a mark to a platform
blocks.body:
The anniversary then became content. Over a hundred filmed interviews with Hong Kong business leaders, indexed and browsable by field — a body of leadership insight rather than a commemorative page.

Designing the identity and building the platform in the same hands meant the site was laid out around what the interviews actually were, not around a template.

projects.title: A Mark Built From People
projects.summary: A full identity for a Hong Kong nursing agency — a mark drawn from human figures arranged into a care cross, documented with construction, type and colour rules, and applied from ID badge to bilingual website.

credits.name: CAREARCH HK 善延護理有限公司

blocks.heading: The mark is the service
blocks.body:
A nursing agency places people. So the mark is made of people — figures arranged into the plus of a care symbol, each one a different colour because the whole point is that they are individuals being matched to a family.

It reads as a medical cross at a glance and as a group of people the moment you look properly.

blocks.caption: Primary logo, and the grid it is built on

blocks.heading: Documented so it survives
blocks.body:
Construction and clear space on a grid. DFYuanHK for the Chinese, tracked +100; Gotham Bold for the Latin, tracked +10. A five-colour system. Three icon treatments and four secondary lockups, so there is a correct answer for a badge, a favicon, an English-only context and a stacked one.

This is the part clients skip and then quietly regret. An agency's brand gets applied by nurses, coordinators and printers — never by the designer.

blocks.caption: Type, colour, and the secondary set

projects.title: House Builder
projects.summary: A 3D-built promotional game world for Milwaukee — modelled tools, wood and plank textures, level art and the UI that carries the brand into a game without diluting it.

blocks.heading: A power-tool brand, in a game
blocks.body: House Builder puts Milwaukee's tools in a player's hands to build houses. A tool brand in a game only survives if the tools read as the real product — the moment a chainsaw becomes a generic game asset, the whole thing stops being Milwaukee and becomes an advert for nobody.

blocks.alt: House Builder key visual with tools and timber house
blocks.caption: Key visual

blocks.heading: Every texture is a product decision
blocks.body:
Levels are named after timber — spruce, oak, redwood, kauri — and each has its own plank and grain treatment, because the difference between woods is the difference between which tool you reach for.

The tool cards carry the real M18 line-up. The action set — fastening, cutting, cleaning — maps to product categories rather than game verbs.

blocks.caption: Texture study, tool UI, level progression

blocks.heading: Modelled, lit, rendered, animated
blocks.body: 3D modelling, game visual design, motion graphics and rendering, all in one pipeline — which is what let the marketing renders and the in-game art stay the same object rather than two interpretations of it.

projects.title: Pocket, Capsule, Mini
projects.summary: 3D product key visuals for the sun-protection brand's umbrella lines — 口袋系列, 膠囊系列 and 小黑傘系列 — each series given its own colour world while staying one family.

blocks.heading: One product, three arguments
blocks.body:
Three umbrella series, each sold on a different claim — pocket-sized and ultralight, capsule in a range of colours, the mini black umbrella blocking 99% of UV. The same object photographed three ways would have made them look like the same thing.

Built in 3D instead: each series gets its own colour world, light and set of floating forms, so a shopper can tell the lines apart at a glance while the brand still reads as one.

items.alt: 小黑傘系列 — mini black umbrella

blocks.heading: Why render rather than shoot
blocks.body: A studio shoot fixes you to the samples that exist on the day. Rendering means the whole range can be shown in every colourway, at a consistent light and scale, before the range is even finished.

projects.title: One Step, One Heart
projects.client: Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital 養和醫院
projects.summary: 一步一愛心 — a four-character 3D cast built in Blender for HKSH's 2023 charity walk, specified tightly enough that the hospital can run the campaign again without the characters drifting.

cover.alt: The four characters walking through the inflatable start arch under the 一步一愛心 lockup

blocks.heading: 一步一愛心
blocks.body:
HKSH's 2023 charity walk asked people to turn up on a morning and walk — one step, one heart. What the campaign needed was not a poster but a cast: four figures who could carry it across registration, route signage, social posts and the finish arch, and still read as the same four people in every one of them.

So we built four characters in Blender rather than illustrating a scene. A scene gets used once. A cast can be re-posed, re-lit and re-shot for whatever the next walk turns out to be.

items.alt: The four characters standing together on the studio ground — the reference lineup
The four walking through a city street scene

blocks.caption: The canon lineup, and the same four dropped into a street

blocks.heading: Four walkers, one silhouette apart
blocks.body:
The cast is spread deliberately across the ages that actually turn up to a hospital walk: a man in his twenties, a woman in her late teens, a woman in her thirties, a man in his sixties. Eighteen centimetres separate the tallest from the shortest, so the lineup has a shape rather than four copies at different scales.

Each one is separated by a single memorable detail and nothing more — a tousled side-swept fringe, a high ponytail with a lime scrunchie, shoulder-length waves, matte black round-rectangle glasses. One feature each is enough to tell them apart at thumbnail size, and few enough that any of them can be rebuilt from the specification alone. Their order in the lineup is fixed and never changes.

items.alt: The character in the Blender viewport, mid-build
A character exported on transparency, ready to composite

blocks.heading: Everything else is identical, on purpose
blocks.body:
All four wear exactly the same kit: a lime felt polo with a grey ribbed collar and a two-button placket, the 養和 calligraphy on the wearer's left chest, a white figure-with-heart pictogram on the lower right hem, periwinkle joggers, lime sneakers with three white stripes.

The faces run on rules rather than drawing decisions — solid black almond eyes with no iris, whites or catchlight, thick black brows, and a single continuous white band for teeth with no lip line and no mouth cavity. It reads austere written down. On screen it is the thing that stops four characters slowly becoming eight.

blocks.alt: The key visual — the four coming through the start arch in the hospital's green and gold
blocks.caption: The arch takes the hospital's own green and gold; the cast supplies everything else

blocks.heading: Written down, so it survives the year
blocks.body:
The part that mattered most was the split. The characters are permanent — proportions, uniform, face rules and colour values are canon and do not move. The campaign sits on top as a layer: the year, the slogan, the arch, the lockups. Change the layer and the same four turn up for the next walk.

So the deliverable was never four model files. It was a turnaround for every character, a colour value for every surface, and a written rule for every part of the face — the kind of specification a team can hand to whoever builds the next round and still get the same four people back.

items.alt: The four characters together, front on
Turnaround — front, three-quarter, side and back
Turnaround — front, three-quarter, side and back
Turnaround — front, three-quarter, side and back
Turnaround — front, three-quarter, side and back

blocks.caption: Model sheets — four views each, so nothing has to be guessed later

projects.title: Irish Chaplaincy
projects.summary: A rebrand for the London charity that has supported excluded, vulnerable and isolated Irish people in Britain since 1957 — replacing a Celtic crest with a three-strand mark, and carrying it through to the website.

cover.alt: Irish Chaplaincy mark and colour palette

blocks.heading: A crest that had stopped travelling
blocks.body:
The Irish Chaplaincy has looked after Irish people in Britain since 1957 — prisoners, Travellers, and older emigrants who came over for work and grew old a long way from home.

The old identity was a circular Celtic crest: knotwork, a green map of Britain and Ireland, and the words Cúram an Deoraí, care of the exile. It said the right thing, but it said it in a form that had stopped moving. Fine letterpressed on a card; illegible at the size of an app icon, a Twitter avatar, a lanyard or a van door. And read quickly by someone who did not already know the charity, a map of two islands inside a ring looks like heritage — not like a service you could ring today.

blocks.alt: The old Celtic crest beside the new three-strand mark
blocks.caption: Old to new

blocks.heading: Three strands, drawn as one line
blocks.body:
The new mark is three leaf shapes turning around a shared centre — a shamrock and a trefoil knot at the same time, so the Irishness survives the modernising instead of being deleted by it.

It also carries the structure of the organisation. Three services — prisoners, Travellers, seniors — each with its own colour, overlapping rather than sitting in separate boxes. Because the shapes are open strokes rather than filled panels, the mark holds together at favicon size and still has air in it at the top of a wall.

The palette gives each strand a light and a deep tone: green #9FCB3A / #50A447, warm orange #E0AE3A / #E95E24, blue #79C9ED / #30789F, with the wordmark in neutral grey so no single service outranks the others. That two-step is what makes the system work in practice — the light tone for large areas, the deep one for type and rules that still have to pass contrast.

items.alt: Irish Chaplaincy mark and hex palette
The mark on a pale ground

blocks.caption: The mark, and the palette it generates

blocks.heading: From a logo to something the charity could run
blocks.body:
A small charity does not need a brand book it will never open; it needs a set of decisions it can repeat without a designer in the room. So the identity was handed over as a working system — the three colour pairs, the grey wordmark, and a way of using the strand colours to signpost each service across the site.

The website put it to work: colour-washed section headers, the three services as the spine of the navigation, and the two things the charity actually needs from a visitor — donate and volunteer — pinned where they can always be reached, on phone and desktop alike.

It has held. The mark is still in use, the charity is still working, and it is heading for its seventieth year.

blocks.alt: Irish Chaplaincy website shown on a monitor, laptop and phone
blocks.caption: The site, across desktop, laptop and phone

projects.title: Pride in Perseverance
projects.summary: Campaign identity for the 52nd Distinguished Salesperson Award — one crystalline key visual carried through stage backdrop, digital panels, banners, brochures, invitations and the award itself.

blocks.heading: 功在不捨，傲而不凡
blocks.body: Campaign identity for the 52nd Distinguished Salesperson Award — Pride in Perseverance. An awards programme is a stress test for a key visual: it has to hold at the scale of a stage backdrop and at the size of a medal ribbon, in two languages, on the same day.

blocks.heading: One visual, every surface
blocks.body: Stage backdrop, digital panels, roll-up banners, the winners' brochure, invitations, and the award itself. Each one is a different production process with a different tolerance, so the visual was built from elements that could be separated and re-weighted rather than a single fixed composition.

projects.title: Always-On
projects.role: Key Visual, Social & Campaign Design, Video Edit
projects.summary: An always-on design partnership with one of Hong Kong's largest health brands — social ads, offer posts, EDMs and TVC cutdowns produced week after week across several product lines, held together by one visual system.

cover.alt: 更年一身輕 key visual for Vita Green Menopause 更年輕

blocks.heading: Not one campaign — a production line
blocks.body:
Vita Green runs a large stable of products, and each one needs a steady stream of work: key visuals, Facebook and Instagram offer posts, carousel ads, EDMs and newsletters, omnichat offer images, e-shop and shopping-mall banners, tent cards and print ads, plus TVC edits and the 15s / 5s cutdowns that follow them.

The brief is rarely "make a campaign". It is closer to: this product, this offer, this week, in eleven placements. Across 2024 and 2025 that has meant a continuous run of jobs rather than a single launch — including the 2025 social media guideline the ongoing work is now built on.

blocks.alt: Menopause 更年輕 poster, offer banner and video still
blocks.caption: 更年輕 — key visual, offer banner and TVC still

blocks.heading: One system, two very different rooms
blocks.body:
更年輕 speaks to women managing menopause, so it is warm and daylit — pink-lavender, soft cream, two women who look like each other's friends. 寧心 is about sleep, so it lives at night: deep navy, gold, a moon.

What holds them together is not colour but structure. The claim sits top-left at a fixed weight, the pack sits at the same optical size in every format, the offer badge is a gold-edged component rather than a red sticker, and the retailer strip closes the frame. Once that grid is settled, a new offer post is a swap, not a redesign — which is the only way a weekly cadence survives.

blocks.alt: Three Vita Calm social posts including the smartwatch gift-with-purchase
blocks.caption: 寧心 Vita Calm — social posts, from clinical claim to the gift-with-purchase

blocks.heading: Evidence, offer, and something to recognise
blocks.body:
Hong Kong health retail argues with numbers — 近90% 醫護用家見證, 3星期, 10天, No.1 — and every post has to carry one without becoming a spec sheet. The number gets the largest type; the ingredient story and the pack sit under it as support; the price and the gift-with-purchase are given their own component so they can change weekly without disturbing anything above them.

The third register is human: a mother and son at the kitchen table, a woman who has stopped fanning herself. In a feed of white-background supplement ads, the recognisable moment is what stops the thumb — the claim is what closes it.

projects.title: Love Work
projects.summary: An ongoing engagement with the architecture practice — the APAC monthly report as motion graphics, an animated argument for working from any location, project films for client presentations, and internal award banners.

blocks.heading: First Friday
blocks.body: The APAC marketing group presents a monthly report. Turning it into motion graphics was the first piece of motion work for Benoy — a recurring format rather than a one-off film, which means it has to be quick to rebuild every month and still look deliberate.

blocks.heading: Love Work
blocks.body:
Benoy put forward a position on the post-COVID work environment: that work happens from any location. It needed a presentation and an animated video to argue it.

The animation had to carry an argument rather than decorate one — isometric diagrams that show what actually changes when an office stops being a single address.

blocks.heading: Project films and award banners
blocks.body: Films for a run of architectural projects, cut for presenting to clients. And internal banners announcing the projects that had won architectural prizes — small work, but it is what a practice's own people see every day.

projects.title: A Dehumidifier You Wear
projects.summary: Retail campaign for a Japanese-made health patch — a celebrity endorsement, three benefit claims and two product variants, held together by one idea a shopper understands in a second.

blocks.heading: 貼上身之抽濕機
blocks.body:
A patch that draws damp out of the body is a hard thing to sell in a sentence. 貼上身之抽濕機 — a dehumidifier you stick on — does it in five characters, and the whole poster is built to deliver that line rather than to list features.

告別水腫 · 回復幼腿 · 改善酸痛 arrive as soft bubbles around it, so the benefits support the idea instead of competing with it.

blocks.heading: Endorsement, accreditation, and two SKUs
blocks.body:
Hong Kong health retail runs on trust markers: a celebrity user, an association accreditation, 日本製造. Each needs its own place in the hierarchy or they cancel each other out.

The two variants — 竹酢 and 唐辛子 — are shown as packs rather than as flat swatches, and the 3D foot and hand renders show where the thing actually goes. That last part matters more than it sounds: most shoppers have never used one.

projects.title: Fifteen Years
projects.summary: Anniversary identity and collateral for the skincare brand — retail display, leaflets, brochures and a social system that keeps the range looking like one family.

blocks.heading: Fifteen years, one shelf
blocks.body: An anniversary mark for a skincare brand, extended across retail display, leaflets, brochures and social. Beauty collateral fails in a specific way: every product gets its own treatment until the range stops looking like one brand on the shelf.

blocks.heading: A family, not a set of one-offs
blocks.body: The system fixes the proportions, the colour behaviour and the type relationship, so a new product or a new promotion joins the family instead of restarting it.

projects.title: The Tool Suite
projects.summary: A suite of hand-built, single-file web tools that let a marketing team across nine cities produce on-brand collateral without a designer in the room.

blocks.heading: The problem
blocks.body:
Nine cities, one brand, and a marketing team that needed a one-pager by Thursday. Every request routed through a designer, so every request waited — and the further from head office, the longer the wait and the looser the brand.

The fix was not a template library. Templates get edited until they are not templates.

blocks.caption: Brand rules enforced by the tool, not by review

blocks.heading: Make the brand the easy path
blocks.body:
Each tool is a single self-contained HTML file. It holds the type, colour, spacing and logo rules, and it will not produce something off-brand because there is no control that lets it.

A marketer fills in the content, the tool does the design. The output is on-brand because it could not have been anything else.

blocks.text: The brand stops being a document people are asked to read, and becomes the shape of the tool they are already using.
blocks.attribution: The idea the suite runs on

projects.title: 小小助養人計劃
projects.client: S.K.H. St. Christopher's Home 聖公會聖基道兒童院
projects.role: Artwork & Production Support (to the Home's design direction)
projects.summary: Assisting on the key visual and the charity chocolate packaging for the children's home's sponsorship programme in its ninetieth year — the Home set the direction, I made the artwork work and got it through production.

cover.alt: 小小助養人計劃 童愛傳承 leaflet

blocks.heading: Someone else's direction, made to work
blocks.body:
小小助養人計劃, the Little Sponsor Programme, under the line 童愛傳承 — the Home has been looking after children in Hong Kong since 1935, and 2025 is its ninetieth year.

The Home had its own direction for how this should look, which is often the case with a charity that knows its families better than any studio ever will. My part was the making: the key visual artwork, the chocolate packaging, and getting both through production.

That is a different job from designing it, and worth saying plainly. A campaign can be entirely decided before it reaches you and still live or die on whether the artwork actually holds — whether the ask stays readable next to the photograph, whether the sponsor line survives being reduced to a leaflet corner, whether the files behave at the printer.

blocks.heading: The children drew it; the job was to keep it theirs
blocks.body:
The charity chocolate is sold to support the programme, and the artwork on it is by the children of the Home — two of them riding a unicorn through the stars on the gift box, a girl in a red dress and a mushroom hat on the pouch, and a different drawing on every individual wrapper.

Production is where that kind of artwork usually gets quietly flattened. Children's drawings are drawn at one size, in soft pencil and marker, with lines that thin out and colours that do not separate. They have to end up on a paper pouch, a rigid box and a wrapper a few centimetres across, printed by three different processes, and still look like a child drew them rather than like a brand imitating one.

So the work was trapping, redrawing and rebuilding the line art for each substrate, keeping the wobble that makes it real, and holding the star motif and the peach edge steady across the set so a box, a bag and a single square read as one thing on a table.

blocks.alt: The campaign leaflet, charity chocolate box, pouch, wrappers and order form
blocks.caption: Leaflet, gift box, pouch, wrappers and the order form

projects.title: 樂胰同樂日
projects.role: Theme & Key Visual, 3D, Game Booth Design, Motion Graphics, Print
projects.summary: The whole theme for HKSH's 2023 diabetes open day — a 3D title, a set of game booths and the motion and print that carried them — built to get people to spend a Saturday afternoon learning about a disease they would rather not think about.

blocks.heading: A pun does the work a warning cannot
blocks.body:
The HKSH Endocrine & Diabetes Centre runs a public open day each year around World Diabetes Day. The 2023 edition — Saturday 4 November, two till five, free — took on the link between diabetes and heart disease.

That is a hard afternoon to sell. Nobody gives up a Saturday to be told what is wrong with them, and the usual health-education look — a red warning triangle, a cross-section of an artery — pushes away exactly the people who most need to walk in.

So the theme starts with a joke. 樂胰同樂日: 胰 is the pancreas, and it sits where 而 would in 樂而同樂 — a fun day for your pancreas. Under it, 糖路與你 從「心」出發, the sugar road and you, setting out from the heart, with the 心 drawn as an actual heart. Two puns, and between them they carry the entire medical message: this is about sugar, this is about your heart, and it is not going to lecture you.

items.alt: The 樂胰同樂日 2023 title modelled in 3D

blocks.caption: The 3D title, and the system it generated

blocks.heading: Sweets, not syringes
blocks.body:
The title was built in 3D rather than set in type — glossy translucent spheres, soft clouds and little plus signs, in green, teal, amber, violet and pink. It reads as boiled sweets and balloons, which for a diabetes campaign is a deliberate risk and the whole point: the thing people are frightened of, made into the thing that gets them through the door.

The same world runs through everything else. The leaflet sits over a small isometric city in the same candy palette, so the programme, the backdrop, the easel signs and the booths are visibly one afternoon rather than five separate print jobs. Motion versions carried it onto screens.

blocks.heading: Games that leave a number behind
blocks.body:
The floor was a set of game booths, each one built around a single thing a visitor could take away.

捉走膽固醇 — catch the cholesterol — is a scored wall of food. Every dish is a photograph in a ring: green and a plus for broccoli, oats, apple, tofu; red and a minus for luncheon meat, fatty pork, crisps, cake. Players pick what they actually ate and add it up. Nobody has to be told what the number means.

我的血糖機 puts a real glucose meter in visitors' hands, and 糖尿病小知識 handles the questions people are too embarrassed to ask a doctor. The stands are modular and repeatable — the same kit works in a lobby, a corridor or a hall — because the people running them on the day are nurses and volunteers, not a design team.

projects.title: Jann Global Logistics
projects.summary: A complete identity for a freight company — mark, typographic spec, a custom set of 3D logistics icons, colour system and full stationery.

blocks.heading: A freight company that had to look like one
blocks.body: A complete identity for a logistics business — mark, typographic specification, colour system and full stationery, documented so it could be used without asking.

blocks.heading: Icons as part of the system
blocks.body: Logistics companies drown in stock icons that never match. This one got a custom set, modelled in 3D and lit consistently, so a diagram of a service reads as the same brand as the letterhead.

projects.title: Keeping the Songs
projects.summary: Bilingual identity and performance content for a London Cantonese opera association — logo lockups in Chinese and English, stage films and a social system for a four-hundred-year-old art form.

blocks.heading: Two scripts, one voice
blocks.body: Identity and performance content for a London Cantonese opera association. The mark had to work in Chinese and English without one being a translation of the other — 昇平粵苑 set to sit beside its English lockup as an equal, not a subtitle.

blocks.alt: 昇平粵苑 logo lockups, Chinese and English
blocks.caption: Bilingual lockups

blocks.heading: The stage is the campaign
blocks.body: For a four-hundred-year-old art form, the argument for an audience is made by the performance itself. The content system is built around stage photography and film rather than graphics about opera.

projects.title: A Voice for Fine Wine
projects.summary: A bilingual content system for the oldest fine-wine house in America — one voice across Instagram and RedNote, in two languages, without sounding translated.

blocks.heading: The problem
blocks.body:
Fine wine copy defaults to two failure modes: auction-catalogue dryness, or the kind of florid tasting-note prose nobody under fifty reads. Acker needed to sound like a two-hundred-year-old house that still goes to dinner.

And it needed to work twice — English on Instagram, Chinese on RedNote — where a straight translation reads as a straight translation.

blocks.text: Say the wine, say why it matters, stop.
blocks.attribution: The rule the whole system runs on

blocks.heading: Written twice, not translated once
blocks.body: RedNote posts are written natively in Chinese against their own platform conventions. The two languages share a position and a set of rules, not a source text.

projects.title: Landing in Tokyo
projects.summary: Market-entry collateral for two new Tokyo centres — drawn network maps, bilingual one-pagers, and a launch page built in a week.

blocks.heading: One week, no photography
blocks.body: Two new Tokyo centres, a launch date that had already been announced, and no photography yet. The drawn network map became the hero because it was the one asset that did not depend on a shoot.

projects.title: Seven Scenes
projects.summary: A scroll-driven cinematic where the page scrub drives a single continuous camera through seven worlds — each one rebuilt from a real project.

blocks.heading: One camera, no cuts
blocks.body:
Scroll position drives video time. The camera flies out of one world and into the next without a cut, so the whole portfolio reads as a single take.

The constraint is what makes it: if you cannot cut, every transition has to be designed rather than edited.
